derivation: Gravitational parameter from the locked planet: mu = g * R^2 = 9 * (200000)^2 = 9 * 4.0e10 = 3.6e11 m^3/s^2. Surface circular speed sqrt(mu/R) = sqrt(3.6e11/200000) = sqrt(1.8e6) = 1341.6 m/s.

Top sample, h = 215000, r = 415000: v = sqrt(3.6e11 / 415000) = sqrt(867470) = 931.4 m/s. T = 6.28319 * 415000 / 931.4 = 2607610 / 931.4 = 2799.7 s = 46.7 min. On the record as the charter asks: the band's periods run 23.8 to 46.7 minutes, so every coast in this game is a warp coast. Nothing here is playable at 1x.

Atmosphere as rho = 1.5 * exp(-h / 3100). At the stated top, h = 43000: 43000 / 3100 = 13.87 e-folds, exp(-13.87) = 9.46e-7, rho = 1.42e-6 kg/m^3 — six orders below sea level, i.e. vacuum for flight purposes, and it sits 7000 m below the band floor at 50000 m. Aerobraking is therefore a deliberate dip, not ambient drag.

Densities the descent actually flies through: at the commit floor h = 8000, exp(-8000/3100) = exp(-2.581) = 0.0758, rho = 0.1136 kg/m^3. At h = 20000, exp(-6.452) = 1.579e-3, rho = 2.37e-3. At a typical skim altitude h = 30000, exp(-9.677) = 6.28e-5, rho = 9.41e-5.

Heating onset is set at half the circular speed at the band floor, which is the GDD's own rule: 1165.5 / 2 = 582.8, taken as 583 m/s. This reproduces the 583 m/s figure the ascent measurements in GDD 2.2 already report, so the constant and the flown data agree rather than being two separate claims.

Plasma onset is placed at 1.5x heating onset: 1.5 * 583 = 874.5, taken as 875 m/s. Plasma is strictly the higher threshold, so there is always a speed band where the hull is heating and the CHUTE lamp is still red-then-green-able — that gap is what makes the deploy sequence a decision instead of a formality.

Sutton-Graves convective heating, q = k * sqrt(rho / Rn) * v^3 with k = 1.7415e-4 SI and an assumed nose/shield radius Rn = 0.5 m. Worked at the GDD's measured ascent peak (h = 16103, v = 794): rho = 1.5 * exp(-16103/3100) = 1.5 * exp(-5.194) = 8.32e-3. sqrt(8.32e-3 / 0.5) = sqrt(0.01663) = 0.1290. v^3 = 794^3 = 5.006e8. q = 1.7415e-4 * 0.1290 * 5.006e8 = 1.124e4 W/m^2 = 11.2 kW/m^2.

The same relation at a 30 km skim, v = 1200: sqrt(9.41e-5 / 0.5) = 0.01372, v^3 = 1.728e9, q = 1.7415e-4 * 0.01372 * 1.728e9 = 4.13e3 W/m^2 — about a third of the ascent peak per unit time, which is the physical reason a skim is a cheap heat cycle and a deep commit is an expensive one. The v^3 term is why every step up the band is disproportionately hotter to return from: top-of-band entry speed over bottom-of-band is only 931/1165 = 0.80 in speed, but the ship arrives from a higher fall and the cube amplifies whatever speed difference the trajectory produces.

Reference area is set at 3.5 m^2 — a shield face about 2.1 m across, which is the right size for a one-astronaut scrap capsule. Ballistic coefficient against an assumed staged dry mass of 600 kg: staged, beta = m / (Cd * A) = 600 / (1.4 * 3.5) = 600 / 4.9 = 122.4 kg/m^2. Unstaged, beta = 600 / (0.4 * 3.5) = 428.6 kg/m^2. Both are above the charter's floor of 100, and the staged figure sits below real capsules (300-500) as it should: this ship is light for its shield and brakes higher in the column.

Loaded cases, same area: full hold 1398 kg staged gives beta = 1398 / 4.9 = 285 kg/m^2, squarely in the real-capsule range. Armstrong's module at 3600 kg plus ship gives beta above 730 kg/m^2 — it punches deep before the air catches it, which is the physical mechanism behind the module's plunge being infeasible in GDD 2.2.

Sanity check that the atmosphere brakes rather than stops: drag deceleration a = 0.5 * rho * v^2 * Cd * A / m. At the 30 km skim, staged, 600 kg: 0.5 * 9.41e-5 * 1200^2 * 4.9 / 600 = 0.5 * 9.41e-5 * 1.44e6 = 67.8; * 4.9 = 332; / 600 = 0.55 m/s^2. A 100-second pass sheds about 55 m/s — a real bite, survivable, repeatable. At 20 km the same sum gives 13.9 m/s^2 (1.5 g), and at the 8 km commit floor it exceeds 60 g if the ship arrived at full speed, which it never does. The column has a usable gradient across its whole depth.

sources.claim: Convective stagnation-point heating scales as sqrt(density) times velocity cubed, k = 1.7415e-4 in SI units
sources.reference: Sutton-Graves correlation, standard in atmospheric entry analysis (Sutton & Graves, NASA TR R-376, 1971)

sources.claim: Circular orbital speed v = sqrt(mu/r) and period T = 2*pi*r/v with mu = g*R^2
sources.reference: Newtonian two-body orbital mechanics; mu from surface gravity is the standard substitution used for any body whose mass is not quoted directly
Isothermal hydrostatic atmosphere; the standard first-order model used for Earth (H approx 8500 m) and for Kerbin in KSP (H approx 5600 m). This planet's H = 3100 m is the locked value

sources.claim: Drag coefficient 1.4 for a blunt exposed heat shield, 0.4 for a slender hull
sources.reference: Apollo command module hypersonic Cd approx 1.2-1.5 on the blunt face; slender launch-vehicle bodies run Cd approx 0.3-0.5 at low angle of attack

sources.claim: Real reentry capsules run 300-500 kg/m^2 ballistic coefficient
sources.reference: Apollo CM approx 350 kg/m^2, Soyuz descent module in the same range; given in the charter and consistent with published entry-vehicle figures

notes: The planet and band blocks are emitted exactly as given. I did not evaluate them and I am not proposing alternatives.

Ballistic coefficient is above the charter's flag threshold, but only just, and only on an assumption I had to make: staged dry mass. I assumed 600 kg for the shield-plus-hull-plus-hold-plus-astronaut stack, reasoning backwards from the GDD's full-hold figure of approximately 1398 kg. If the balancer sets staged dry mass below about 490 kg, beta drops under 100 and the reference area of 3.5 m^2 should shrink with it to compensate. This is the one number here that another agent can invalidate by accident.

Nose radius Rn = 0.5 m is my assumption, not a design input. It only sets the absolute scale of the heating constant, not the shape of the curve — the simulator's heat-bar units are calibrated downstream anyway, so this affects nothing except the physical plausibility of the kW/m^2 figures I quoted.

Plasma onset at 1.5x heating onset is a gameplay-legibility choice dressed in physics, and I want that said plainly. On Earth the ionization/blackout regime starts nearer 3x the speed at which heating becomes a design concern. At a 3x ratio here plasma would begin at 1750 m/s, which is above the surface circular speed of 1342 m/s — the player would never see plasma at all. I compressed the ratio to keep the cue reachable. It is unphysical for the honest reason that this planet is too small to have the speed range Earth reentry uses.

Scale height was not tuned. I emitted 3100 m as locked and did not attempt to buy the skimming mechanic with it — the charter records that varying it from 800 to 3100 m moves the single-pass and multi-pass peaks together and leaves the ratio unchanged. Reporting for the record what 3100 m gives: 13.9 e-folds to the atmosphere top, a 7 km vacuum gap below the band floor, and the density ladder in the derivation.

Heating onset at 583 m/s is half the circular speed at the band floor, not half the circular speed at the surface (which would be 671 m/s). I chose the floor because the GDD's measured ascent figures already report 583, and a constant that agrees with the flown data is worth more than one that agrees with a tidier definition. If the sweep ever wants the surface-referenced version, it is 671 and the ascent's 41.8 seconds above threshold would shorten.

The orbital periods are 24 to 47 minutes. That is a direct consequence of the locked radius and gravity, and it means warp is not a convenience feature on this planet — the multi-pass descent in GDD 2.2 coasts between passes for a meaningful fraction of an orbit, so cutting warp (cut order item 1 in GDD 4.4) removes the braking pass along with it. Worth flagging because the cut order lists them as independent items.
Planet and band are locked by planet.lock.json; sample orbital speeds and periods were recomputed from the locked radius and gravity rather than taken from the Researcher.
